units.title: Logic
units.blurb: Read and build compound statements, truth tables, quantifiers and valid arguments.

units.title: Proof Techniques
units.blurb: Test claims with counterexamples, then set up direct, contrapositive, case-by-case and contradiction arguments.

units.title: Sets and Functions
units.blurb: Describe collections precisely, combine them, and study functions between them.

units.title: Relations
units.blurb: Describe how elements are related, sort them into classes, and put them in order.

units.title: Counting
units.blurb: Count arrangements and selections without listing them: rules, complements, inclusion–exclusion, stars and bars, and pigeonholes.

units.title: Induction, Recursion and Growth
units.blurb: Prove statements for every whole number, set up and solve recurrence relations, and compare how fast functions grow.

units.title: Graph Theory
units.blurb: Model connections with graphs: degrees, paths and circuits, trees, shortest routes, coloring and planarity.

topics.title: Statements and Connectives
topics.short: A statement is either true or false; "and," "or" and "not" build new statements from old ones.
topics.trouble: Students read "or" as "one or the other but not both." In math, "P or Q" is also true when both are true.

topics.title: Truth Tables
topics.short: List every combination of truth values, 2ⁿ rows for n statements, and work out the compound statement one column at a time.
topics.trouble: Students list fewer than 2ⁿ rows and miss a case.

topics.title: The Conditional and the Biconditional
topics.short: P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false; P ↔ Q is true when P and Q have the same truth value.
topics.trouble: Students mark P → Q false whenever P is false. A false hypothesis makes the conditional true: a promise whose condition never happened was not broken.

topics.title: Logical Equivalence and De Morgan's Laws
topics.short: Two statements are equivalent when their truth tables match: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q.
topics.trouble: Students negate "P and Q" as "not P and not Q," or treat a conditional as equivalent to its converse instead of its contrapositive.

topics.title: Quantifiers
topics.short: "For all" (∀) and "there exists" (∃) make claims about every element of a domain, or about at least one.
topics.trouble: Students forget that the domain matters: ∃x (x² = 2) is true for real numbers and false for rational numbers.

topics.title: Negating Quantified Statements
topics.short: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).
topics.trouble: Students negate "all of them are" as "none of them are." The negation is "at least one is not."

topics.title: Nested Quantifiers
topics.short: The order of ∀ and ∃ matters: ∀x ∃y (y > x) is true for real numbers, but ∃y ∀x (y > x) is false.
topics.trouble: Students swap the order of mixed quantifiers as if it changed nothing.

topics.title: Valid Arguments and Rules of Inference
topics.short: Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid forms of argument; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are not.
topics.trouble: Students accept "If P, then Q. Q is true, so P is true." That is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

topics.title: Disproving with a Counterexample
topics.short: One case where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails disproves a "for all" claim.
topics.trouble: Students offer examples that agree with a claim as if they proved it, or a "counterexample" that does not satisfy the hypothesis.

topics.title: Direct Proof
topics.short: Assume the hypothesis, rewrite it with definitions (an even number is 2k), and reason step by step to the conclusion.
topics.trouble: Students check a few numbers and call that a proof, or write two different even numbers as 2k and 2k with the same k.

topics.title: Proof by Contrapositive
topics.short: To prove P → Q, prove ¬Q → ¬P instead: to show "if n² is even, then n is even," show that odd n gives odd n².
topics.trouble: Students prove the converse Q → P by mistake, which is a different statement.

topics.title: Proof by Cases
topics.short: Split into cases that cover every possibility (n even or odd; n = 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2) and prove each one.
topics.trouble: Students leave out a case, such as zero or the negative numbers.

topics.title: Proof by Contradiction
topics.short: Assume the statement is false and reason to something impossible, as in the proof that √2 is irrational.
topics.trouble: Students start from a wrong negation of the statement, so the contradiction they reach proves nothing.

topics.title: Sets and Set-Builder Notation
topics.short: Describe a set by listing its elements or by a rule, and use ∈, ⊆ and |A|.
topics.trouble: Students mix up ∈ and ⊆: 1 ∈ {1, 2} but {1} ⊆ {1, 2}. Also ∅ and {∅} are different sets: the second has one element.

topics.title: Set Operations
topics.short: Union, intersection, difference and complement, pictured with Venn diagrams, with De Morgan's laws for sets.
topics.trouble: Students take the complement of A ∩ B to be Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ instead of Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ.

topics.title: Power Sets and Cartesian Products
topics.short: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, and A × B has |A| · |B| ordered pairs.
topics.trouble: Students leave ∅ and the whole set out of the list of subsets, or treat the ordered pair (a, b) as the set {a, b}.

topics.title: Functions Between Sets
topics.short: A function assigns each element of its domain exactly one element of its codomain; the range is the set of outputs actually reached.
topics.trouble: Students use "codomain" and "range" as if they meant the same set.

topics.title: One-to-One and Onto Functions
topics.short: One-to-one: different inputs give different outputs. Onto: every element of the codomain is reached.
topics.trouble: Students decide without looking at the domain and codomain, but f(x) = x² is one-to-one and onto from [0, ∞) to [0, ∞) and neither from the real numbers to the real numbers.

topics.title: Bijections and Inverse Functions
topics.short: A function has an inverse exactly when it is one-to-one and onto, and (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
topics.trouble: Students undo a composition in the order it was applied instead of the reverse order.

topics.title: Relations and Their Properties
topics.short: A relation on A is a set of ordered pairs; check whether it is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive.
topics.trouble: Students think "antisymmetric" means "not symmetric." Equality is both, and some relations are neither.

topics.title: Equivalence Relations and Partitions
topics.short: A reflexive, symmetric and transitive relation splits its set into classes that do not overlap.
topics.trouble: Students forget to check transitivity, or put one element into two different classes.

topics.title: Partial Orders and Hasse Diagrams
topics.short: Draw a partial order such as "divides" as a Hasse diagram, and list the elements in an order that respects it.
topics.trouble: Students draw the edges that transitivity already implies, or assume every two elements must be comparable.

topics.title: The Sum and Product Rules
topics.short: Add the counts of cases that cannot happen together; multiply the counts of choices made one after another.
topics.trouble: Students multiply when the cases are alternatives (either/or) that should be added, or add when the choices are made in sequence.

topics.title: Counting the Complement
topics.short: Count "at least one" as all the possibilities minus the ones with none.
topics.trouble: Students count committees with at least one woman by choosing one woman first and then anyone at all, which counts the same committee several times.

topics.title: Inclusion–Exclusion
topics.trouble: Students subtract the pairwise overlaps but forget to add back the triple overlap.

topics.title: The Division Rule: Repeated Letters and Round Tables
topics.short: Divide out the orderings that look the same: MISSISSIPPI has 11!/(4! · 4! · 2!) arrangements, and n people around a round table have (n − 1)!.
topics.trouble: Students divide by the wrong factorials, or count rotations of the same seating at a round table as different.

topics.title: Pascal's Identity and Counting Arguments
topics.short: Prove an identity by counting one set in two ways: C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k), and each row of Pascal's triangle adds to 2ⁿ.
topics.trouble: Students check an identity for one value of n and call it proved.

topics.title: Lattice Paths and Binary Strings
topics.short: A path of right and up steps is a string of R's and U's, so a grid m steps wide and n steps tall has C(m + n, n) shortest paths.
topics.trouble: Students count grid squares instead of steps, or count the paths through a point by adding the two parts instead of multiplying them.

topics.title: Stars and Bars
topics.short: There are C(n + k − 1, k − 1) ways to put n identical items into k boxes, and C(n − 1, k − 1) when every box gets at least one.
topics.trouble: Students use stars and bars for items that are all different, or forget to hand out the required items first when boxes have a minimum.

topics.title: The Pigeonhole Principle
topics.short: If more than k · n items go into n boxes, some box gets at least k + 1; to guarantee something, plan for the worst case.
topics.trouble: Students find the number that makes a repeat possible instead of the number that guarantees one, which is one more than the worst case.

topics.title: Derangements
topics.short: Count the arrangements where nothing stays in its own place with inclusion–exclusion: D₄ = 9, and Dₙ/n! approaches 1/e.
topics.trouble: Students subtract the arrangements with one item fixed but never correct for the ones with two or more items fixed.

topics.title: Induction for Divisibility and Inequalities
topics.short: Use the case n = k to rewrite the case n = k + 1: 3 ∣ (4ⁿ − 1) for n ≥ 1, and 2ⁿ > n² for n ≥ 5.
topics.trouble: Students start at the wrong base case (2ⁿ > n² fails at n = 2, 3 and 4), or never use the case n = k in the inductive step.

topics.title: Strong Induction
topics.short: Assume every case up to k to prove case k + 1, with as many base cases as the step reaches back.
topics.trouble: Students check one base case when the step reaches back further. Every amount of at least 12¢ can be paid with 4¢ and 5¢ stamps, and the step from n − 4 needs the four base cases 12, 13, 14 and 15.

topics.title: Setting Up Recurrence Relations
topics.short: Describe a count by how it depends on smaller cases: tilings, binary strings with no two 1s in a row, and the Tower of Hanoi.
topics.trouble: Students count only one way the pattern can end (a square tile last) and miss the others, or forget the starting values.

topics.title: Solving Recurrences by Unrolling
topics.short: Substitute the rule into itself until a pattern appears, then check the closed form: aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 1 with a₁ = 1 gives aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1.
topics.trouble: Students guess a formula from the first two terms and never check it against the recurrence.

topics.title: Linear Recurrences with Distinct Roots
topics.short: For aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂, solve r² = c₁r + c₂ and fit aₙ = A·r₁ⁿ + B·r₂ⁿ to the first two terms.
topics.trouble: Students write the characteristic equation with the wrong signs, as r² + c₁r + c₂ = 0, or fit A and B to only one starting value.

topics.title: Linear Recurrences with a Repeated Root
topics.short: When r² = c₁r + c₂ has a double root r, the solutions are aₙ = (A + Bn)rⁿ.
topics.trouble: Students write A·rⁿ + B·rⁿ, which is really one solution and cannot fit two starting values.

topics.title: Growth Rates and Big-O
topics.short: Rank functions by how fast they grow, log n ≪ n ≪ n log n ≪ n² ≪ 2ⁿ ≪ n!; f is O(g) when f(n) ≤ C · g(n) for all large n.
topics.trouble: Students judge growth from small values of n (100n is larger than n² until n = 100), or think a constant factor changes the Big-O class.

topics.title: Graphs, Degrees and the Handshake Lemma
topics.short: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges; the degrees add up to twice the number of edges.
topics.trouble: Students think a graph can have an odd number of vertices of odd degree. The degrees add up to an even number, so it cannot.

topics.title: Complete, Bipartite and Cycle Graphs
topics.short: Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges, K(m, n) has mn, and the cycle Cₙ has n.
topics.trouble: Students count the edges of Kₙ as n(n − 1), counting each edge once from each end.

topics.title: Walks, Paths, Cycles and Connectivity
topics.short: A path never repeats a vertex; a graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path.
topics.trouble: Students mix up walks (repeats allowed), trails (no repeated edges) and paths (no repeated vertices).

topics.title: Adjacency Matrices and Counting Walks
topics.short: Store a graph as a matrix A; the (i, j) entry of Aᵏ counts the walks of length k from i to j.
topics.trouble: Students think Aᵏ counts paths, but the walks it counts may repeat vertices and edges.

topics.title: Graph Isomorphism
topics.short: Two graphs have the same structure when a relabeling of the vertices matches their edges; different degree sequences prove they do not.
topics.trouble: Students decide two graphs are isomorphic because their degree sequences match. Matching invariants is necessary, not enough.

topics.title: Euler Paths and Circuits
topics.short: A connected graph has an Euler circuit when every degree is even, and an Euler path when exactly two degrees are odd.
topics.trouble: Students confuse Euler paths (every edge once) with Hamilton paths (every vertex once), or start an Euler path at a vertex of even degree.

topics.title: Hamilton Paths and Cycles
topics.short: Visit every vertex exactly once; there is no quick test, but Dirac's theorem guarantees a cycle when every degree is at least n/2.
topics.trouble: Students treat Dirac's condition as necessary, but the cycle C₆ is itself a Hamilton cycle, though every degree is only 2.

topics.title: Trees
topics.short: A tree is connected with no cycles; a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges, and adding any edge creates a cycle.
topics.trouble: Students call any graph with n − 1 edges a tree; it must also be connected.

topics.title: Minimum Spanning Trees
topics.short: Kruskal's algorithm adds the cheapest remaining edge that does not close a cycle, until n − 1 edges are chosen.
topics.trouble: Students add the cheapest edge even when it closes a cycle, or stop before they have n − 1 edges.

topics.title: Shortest Paths with Dijkstra's Algorithm
topics.short: Each round, settle the closest unsettled vertex and update the distances of its neighbors.
topics.trouble: Students settle a vertex as soon as they first reach it, before checking whether a route through other vertices is shorter.

topics.title: Graph Coloring
topics.short: Color the vertices so that neighbors differ; a graph can be colored with two colors exactly when it has no odd cycle.
topics.trouble: Students assume a greedy coloring always uses the fewest colors; the result depends on the order of the vertices.

topics.title: Planar Graphs and Euler's Formula
topics.short: A connected planar drawing has v − e + f = 2; since a simple planar graph has e ≤ 3v − 6, K₅ is not planar.
topics.trouble: Students forget to count the outside region as a face, or use e ≤ 3v − 6 to claim a graph is planar, when it can only rule graphs out.
